utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you are to continue your examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the witness will be able to come closer to the map and sit at the same time, because as I understand, there's an extension cable provided for him to be able to speak in the microphone while he is showing things on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so? May I be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the extension is for the headphone, not for the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we're going to face difficulties. But, anyway, let us start working and then we'll see whether it is going to proceed normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, good morning. You know that last time we started this examination-in-chief on behalf of the Defence. In order not to go back to what I had started, I'd like to ask you this: Before you became a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which unit of the JNA you had been a member of?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 216th Mountain Brigade of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how this change occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Yugoslav army withdraw from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 19th of May, 2002, and pursuant to the decision of the assembly of the Republika Srpska on the 12th of May, the army of Republika Srpska was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that this name was given to it? Do you know anything about it in particular or did you not attach any special importance to that under the circumstances when the hostilities broke out?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the media, we learned that the assembly of Republika Srpska had reached a decision to form a new army to be named the army of Republika Srpska and that the chief -- the General Staff was established, headed by General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to go back to what you spoke about last week; however, you do remember that on the day when we started, we left off with your answer in which you said that there were no changes in positions of the two parties, i.e., the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the BH army from 1992 until the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. I said that since 19th December, 1994, when I assumed my duties, there were no changes after that date until the 15th of June, 1995 offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you describe for us the positions in April 1992? For example, on the hills of Zuc, Hum, Grdonj, et cetera, what were the positions like at the time? But please careful to speak in the microphone when you give your answers.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the VRS positions and the positions of the ABiH, or rather, the 1st Corps, looked differently than shown in this map, because Vogosca, Rajlovac route, where Zuc was a dominant feature, were held by the Serbia forces all the way up to the tobacco factory, Potoka Kuca, Pofalici, Naselje, all the way to Hum and the Zuc hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Grdonj is concerned, it's here, and these positions remained unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how the forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The area that you have just mentioned and explained was populated by whom in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pofalici and Zuc were predominantly inhabited by Serbs. They constituted a much bigger majority than the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what happened in that area after the hostilities began?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the hostilities began, on the 16th of May, from the direction of Hum the town, and the Kuco Potok, the population came under attack. They tried to defend themselves in Pofalici, and this area of Pofalici here was lost. The Serb civilians had to leave the area, and the defending soldiers sustained enormous casualties. When on the 16th of May this area was seized, forces were regrouped. I'm talking about the BH army forces, or rather, the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after that they continued with combat operations from the direction of Pofalici, Kuce Potok with a view of capturing, Zuc; and, finally, on the 8th of June, they managed to seize this dominating feature stretching from Vogosca, or rather, Hum, which overlooks Polinje to Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. What was the precise date of those hostilities which led to the loss of that territory by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This took place on the 16th of May, 1992, when Pofalici and the whole neighbourhood of Zuc fell. Since this hilly area was populated, it fell on the 8th of June; and, finally, the Muslim forces took full control of the Zuc feature on the 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that was the date?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was that the date when this separation line was set up?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, what happened with the population in the area, the majority Serb population? Were there any casualties there is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many casualties in the area of Pofalic. According to the census and according to the findings of certain commissions, the number of casualties was almost 300. On the 8th of June, when Zuc was finally seized, the majority of casualties were among soldiers and to a lesser degree among civilians, but their entire property was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in May, who were the casualties?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs in Pofalici and, as I said, almost 300 people were casualties in May. Some people say there were even children among them, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that was the situation to the north. What was happening and who in April 1992 was in the area of the Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1992, the Green Berets were in the area of Mojmilo, including the Territorial Defence and the Patriotic League. I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about April, before the hostilities broke out.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were living in Mojmilo. There were a few Serbs, but it was predominantly populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Mojmilo, there were some facilities like water-tanks. There was a small JNA unit guarding these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I'm putting this question to you. How did it happen that this JNA unit that was there in April in Mojmilo was not there any longer? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a small guard unit, and the Patriotic League, the Territorial Defence, and the Green Berets forced them out by using weapons and other means used in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did this exactly happen?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I do know for sure that between the 3rd and the 10th of May, the armies of the VRS or the JNA were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did the situation on Debelo Brdo and Colina Kapa became the one as you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo and Colina Kapa had positions that remained unchanged between 1992 and the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Under the circumstances, can you explain what was the position of Grbavica, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, and Hrasno? Can you explain their position and where the separation line was?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, or rather, in April of that year, and early May, JNA units and later on, on 19th of May, the VRS units held the airport. We had an axis from Lukavica towards Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that we held both the airport parts of Lukavica, one part of Dobrinja, and Grbavica within the boundaries almost as the ones shown here, although there was some shifting in 1992 towards Grbavica, too. So the positions on Grbavica remained more or less unchanged. There were just some minor shifts here in 1992 in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we're concerned, we moved from the area of Han Pijesak to assist in the evacuation of the army, the 2nd Army that was stationed at Bistrik. We headed out on the 2nd of May; and by the 3rd of May we arrived at Lukavica in the Lukavica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, a lot of mention has been made about protected areas. Can you please us, what was the position of those parts of the town that I just asked you about, in relation to the existence of the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean Grbavica, Nedzarici, Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in early May, no protected areas had been declared yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when this idea was mooted, what can you say in this regard? In view of the position of Grbavica Hrasno, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, was this part of this zone?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't hold Hrasno at all, but we did hold Nedzarici and Grbavica. And as far as I know, there were no protected areas at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the demilitarised zones?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Srebrenica was a demilitarised zone, and Zepa, too. I didn't hear about any other zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Igman?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Igman was declared a demilitarised zone in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only for a very brief period of time and then it was demilitarised no longer because the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: It is impossible to work because we can hear a lot of background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. The interpreter says that it is impossible to work because she's hearing a lot of background noise, and may I ask that this be checked by the technical personnel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Your Honours, this is because of the microphone that was switched on at the Defence bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you understand that? She says that this is because of the microphone that was switched on at the Defence bench, so that microphone is to be turned off. So let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, Witness, to speak slowly. You did so last time, but could you please continue doing so because then we could put everything into the transcript. So could you please tell us what happened with Igman, in light of the fact that it had been declared a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Operation Lukovac 1993 was launched in early July 1993. The units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps reinforced with some other elements from other corps, and from the Main Staff got from their lines at Jahorina to the area of Bjelasnica and the village of Lukavica; and then they established this line towards Grdonj and managed to reach this whole area here at Bjelasnica; and then the United Nations reached a decision whereby the units of the Republika Srpska army and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps should withdraw from the area of Bjelasnica and the large portions of the Igman mountain, and the lines that it could still retain were defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was this complied with?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Republika Srpska army did withdraw to the lines as defined by the UN, because there were threats that there would be air-strikes if it failed to do so; and as far as I know, I was in one of the brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And the Brigades that were here on those positions really had to withdraw, and that's what at the did. They withdrew all the way down to the lines as they were determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who posed a threat to this demilitarised zone after that period and when?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not at the corps command at the time, but we did receive reports, we and the other brigades, that the force of the BH army, the 1st Corps, exploited the fact of our withdrawal and infiltrated the majority of its forces from some of its positions into the mountain of Igman, thus violating the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen? Can you tell us at least approximately?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in the fall of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from that time, until the end of the war, who actually held the positions on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, Mount Igman, to be quite precise, 80 per cent of Mount Igman was held by the BH army forces, the 1st Corps, and one portion of Igman was held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as stipulated in the order and the agreement between the -- our forces and the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And since the BH army held this part of Igman that you just described to us, what areas did it control from those dominant positions if we look at the demarcation line that you explained at length last time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this western area, it controlled this area here. So it didn't move its positions, and the positions were not moved here where they faced the Serbian area of Veljkovici; and then here, the positions were like this, and their forces held these positions and this is how our lines went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I actually asked you something else. From its positions on Mount Igman, the BH army was able to control what areas, when we talk about the demarcation lines?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those positions made it possible for them to control this area Vojkovici. There are about one thousand houses here, all Serbian households; and this line from the foothills of the Igman, all the way down to these villages, they were able to control this area from their dominant positions; in other words, the inhabits of these villages and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps units. And here to the west, they were able to control the Ilidza area; and as for the rest, well, they controlled this area, too, from their dominant positions, but this was just a wooded area

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. We're just trying to understand the import of the evidence, and we wondered whether the witness might be able to say whether he has any information as to why Igman was demilitarised by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was not at the command at that time, but we, in the units, received information to that effect from our brigade commanders. I became a member of the corps on the 19th of December, 1994; and from that time on, I am able to give you more details about the positions of the corps, and I'm familiar with almost everything that happened at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So you don't have any information as to why Igman was demilitarised. You may not have, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in all probability, this was because in 1993 there was Operation Lukovac, and the forces of the 1st Corps of the Republika Srpska army managed to reach those units here -- those positions here at Malo Pojle and Velika Polje at Igman. And all they had to do was to take this kilometre here to, again, establish the encirclement around Sarajevo, and they were not allowed to do that. So the supply lines for the city would have been broken had that been allowed to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just to continue with a follow-up question following the President's question. You arrived in the corps on the 19th of December, 1994, after a decision had been made to demilitarise Igman. When you arrived, who was effectively in command of the place, of Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I joined the corps, as you yourself said, the Muslim forces dominated Mount Igman; in other words, the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, well, the first question: When did the Republika Srpska army lose its control over the airport?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska army, pursuant to a decision of the United Nations and by virtue of signing agreement on the demilitarised zone of the airport, which was to be placed under the control of UNPROFOR, and this was concluded sometime in June, late June or early July 1992 as far as I know, but I -- I'm not sure about the dates. But it was in June or July, that was when the Republika Srpska army forces handed over the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how would you then define the positions of the two sides at that moment after this decision was reached? What is your assessment of the situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we held the airport, which was until June or July 1992, the BH army forces, by that I mean the 1st Corps, they were in the encirclement within the city of Sarajevo. When our forces pulled-out from the airport in June and July, the forces and the population were no longer in the encirclement, and our position became more difficult and we had to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment. Could you please give shorter answers; and if necessary, the Trial Chamber will seek additional clarification. How did the position of the Republika Srpska army deteriorate after it had handed over the airport?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the airport was handed over, the Republika Srpska army found itself in a very difficult situation, in terms of command and control, and in terms of its supply lines, transportation, the evacuation of the wounded and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the Lukavica-Ilidza route?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lukavica-Ilidza route was cut off at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the people from Ilidza, Ilijas, Vogosca, and those areas that were still part of Sarajevo at the time, were they able to go anywhere, to move at all?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from Ilidza, the broader area of Ilidza, and Ilijas were able to move, but it was quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to specify. Don't use pronouns. But have you to name the locations, because we can't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people from Ilijas, since Ilijas is here to the north, they were able to move towards Vogosca. That route was open, the route to Vogosca. But as far as the Vogosca to Grdonj route, we actually had to build a road here through very rugged train, here, all the way through Hrese, and then onwards to Pale. As for Ilidza, the broader area, there was a road to Lukavica, through Vrace to Pale; and when the airport area was handed over, they too had to move to Rajlovac, Vogosca, and then they had to take this very difficult road that we had to build. It was an macadam road that we built.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say difficult road?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this is a macadam road, that it was not a proper road, that the terrain is hilly, and that transportation took a long time, and it was very far away to go the other way around, 50 or 60 kilometres was the other road to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were the other difficulties involved? Were there dangers, towards Spicasta Stijena, elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were dangers since the road went close to the separation lines at the areas of Zuc and Hum and Grdonj, and the Kosova areas, too. So the road could be hit by different weaponry, including mortars, all weapons that had a range of over 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the road could be hit, and what was it that actually happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what often happened on the road was that people got killed on that road because of the gun-fire coming from the other side. It was soldiers who were killed and civilians who moved air long that road, because there was no other road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That road, say, from to Lukavica, how long was it in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where Ilidza is, and then have you to go here, Vogosca, Hrese through Pale, Pale is here, and then only from up here where Trebevic is and then down to Lukavica. So it was 70 or 100 kilometres; whereas, here the road to Lukavica was five to six kilometres. Well, via Nedzarici, it wasn't even three kilometres, viewed from this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about people from Ilijas. Did they have any alternative and how could they go? How else could they leave the area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Ilijas. When they came, they took this other road, Vogosca and here, and then via this road leading to Sokolac. It was a dirt path more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there was practically no road, what were you saying? Can you explain this to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a enormous mountain, and there are woods and certain parts from where timber is taken. These were macadam roads. They weren't proper roads. They were only used for heavy trucks that would transport the timber from there. Ozren is the name of that mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that you should start answering questions when the typing stops; and also when you give your answers when the typing stops, that is when we will continue and would you please try to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit inconvenient for me sitting this way and trying to explain things and point them out. It was much easier in the other courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain whether you know whether a tunnel existed under the airport?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a tunnel under the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that is referred to the indictment against General Milosevic, did it function; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this tunnel functioned from the autumn of 1993 onwards; that is to say, the months of November/December 1993, all of 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what actually went through this tunnel; did you know?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not see; but according to our intelligence, the tunnel was used for manoeuver purposes of the 1st Corps of the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, moving from town towards Igman, and from these positions and to Igman, and then also towards Nisica Vesarevn [phoen], the Niksic plateau, and this other area up here. This tunnel was built over here in this area, and it went into Butmir, Hrasnica, and the Hrasnica road further on. That's where the forces moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the 1st Romanija Brigade. What positions was it in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade in 1992 and 1993 was at these positions: Grbavica, Zlatiste, Trebevic, and here, all the way to Grdonj and Spicasta Stijena, and in part, through Jahorina in this area towards Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the fiercest fighting took place in relation to the separation line?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fiercest fighting took place in the area of Grbavica and here in the area of Nedzarici in 1992, and in view of the fact that there was always fighting in this area, but Nedzarici-Grbavica was where the fiercest fighting took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under these circumstances, can you explain what the position was, especially in relation to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica was in a fire pocket, as we say, facing Miljacka in the urban area. From Mojmilo and from Debelo Brdo, it was exposed to cross-fire. It was encircled by a firing system. Fire came from Mojmilo, Debelo Brdo, and from in here. There was cross-fire, and in addition to that, there was fire from all areas. So it was as if it were a sack that was fired on. That's why we call it a fire sack, too. And fire came from Nedzarici as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the area of Spicasta Stijena and Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Spicasta Stijena and Grdonj, since the main feature of Grdonj, which is when viewed from here, from Radava goes to Hrese or Pasino Brdo. That is where the forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a dominant position and threatened the village of Mrkovici, and that's where the supplies for the Ilidza and for the north-east and part of the front came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At what time period is this that we're talking about? What year is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1992, all the way up to 1995, the lines remained unchanged in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I was going to ask you, Mr. Tapuskovic, whether, having dealt with 1992, you're going to move on to the later period, 1994/1995, which is actually the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. But it was necessary to explain all of this, in relation to these hills and all these problems, because I think that without that I couldn't ask him anything that is related to the relevant time. That is why I thought that, first of all, the witness should tell me the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Lukavica 1993?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukovac 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Lukovac 1993, yes. Were there any similar actions later, with a similar name, except for that particular one that happened then?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no similar action, and the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, in view of the personnel levels, could not have carried out such an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were in these areas, what kind of orders did you receive in terms of opening fire and in which situations could you open fire, according to these instructions or these orders?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me what year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about 1992, but I'm also asking you a general question.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, there were conflicts between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of Republika Srpska in the entire territory here, in relation to the city and further on, the front line; and from February 1994, when there was a demilitarisation of the artillery, when all heavy weaponry had to be taken out, there weren't supposed to be any clashes in the urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that as well. I'm asking but when the hostilities broke out. What kind of orders were issued in relation to when it was possible to take military action.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military action could be taken only if the positions of the army of Republika Srpska were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I will be allowed to show a document, to show the witness a document that was not on my 65 ter list, but it is on the Prosecutor's list for cross-examination. I think that I can avail myself of such a right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 65 ter number is 03140. It's a Prosecution document that I got after the witness took his solemn oath. Could that document please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the English version. Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this document. Please look at its date. Can you tell us what the date is of this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of September, 1992. The command of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Slower, slower, please. What is this?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see. Oh, it's me. It says KIK, Captain First Class, Stevan Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what paragraph 1 says. If you can, read it out and tell us whether that is the way things actually were, but read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the night, the enemy was sporadically opening sniper and infantry arms fire on all defence positions of the brigade." I cannot read a certain part of it. "From 1600 hours, an 82 millimetre mortar was operating on Soping, which resulted in the killing of one civilian; whereas, another civilian was severely wounded in various intervals. An "osa" was operating."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wait and give us your answer slowly. Can you read out paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2: "Units of the brigade respond only in exceptional circumstances with gun-fire when enemy fire reaches such intensity that it endangers the lives of our soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't have you him tell us -- have him tell us or explain to us the references to Soping and osa in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I wanted to ask him after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On whose territory Soping was?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soping was in the territory of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does osa signify?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a firing at the Jewish cemetery held by the Romanija forces. Osa was an anti-rocket launcher intended to destroy bunkers and other armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here you described under which circumstances it was allowed to open fire. Was that the essence of the orders that you were receiving throughout the whole war? Did you receive any different orders in any sense?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 99 per cent of cases, the commanders issued orders only to open fire if we came under attack, not to fire on the enemy and not to provoke any armed conflict. This is the kind of order that we were receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 4, can you please look at it and tell us if what you wrote in this document is true.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see exactly the time, but it says here that in a passage beneath Soping, one killed civilian was found. The case was reported to the military police which has been investigating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct, because this is what I wrote in my report, obviously, but it's been a long time ago and it's difficult for me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like now to show you another document, which is on my list, 65 ter list, but it was also on the Prosecution list, and it's still on the Prosecution list of documents that the Prosecution intends to use with this witness. The number of this 65 ter document is 0169 -- 01969. It's a bit longer document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. While we're waiting, what is the fate of this document the Defence has shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you prompting him to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I'm tendering it as a Defence exhibit to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 03140 becomes D185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is another document. I'm not sure if we have an English version thereof. Can we just move to the end of this document first; that is, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Major-General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you were talking about your combat report. Can you please look at the penultimate passage of your 1992 combat report. Was this combat report in line with what is written here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean item 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the last passage of item 8. Can you please read it? Please, sorry. Can you please read the last passage of item 8?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Envisage and make concrete tasks as to who is to neutralise and destroy fire points, machine-gun, and sniper nests which prevent movement around Grbavica, Ilidza, Vogosca, Kasindol," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, my screen is malfunctioning and I'm not able to follow the cursor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This order, is it in the spirit what you wrote in your combat report?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back now to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please first look at the date? What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at the end of this first page, specifically item 6, or rather, 7, and its last sentence.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please enlarge this a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at it.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Item 4, it begins with, "four" under item 7. It is the last sentence, the very last sentence.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see 7. It's not item 4; it's the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment is to draw up a fire plan in the region of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Mixed Artillery Division of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade is to prepare fire according to the brigade commander's decision. The 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment is to draw up a fire plan in the region of Bascarsija and Vrbanja. Fire is to be open in compliance with the order of the SRK commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now explain to me what was the position of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps throughout the war vis-a-vis Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Bascarsija, this area here, and it's the most important part of the town in the cultural and historical sense. This particular neighbourhood, it was built in the Turkish architectural style with very meager and fragile material. It comprised small houses and buildings. There were only a few artillery shots that would require to destroy this whole area. That is -- that is why these buildings were protected strictly and they remained unchanged and intact to this date, and anyone with verify and check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why such a decision had to be made only with the approval or on orders of the commander of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was particularly stressed and reports were being sent to units, saying that such buildings the civilian population and roads and movements of people shall not be targeted at any cost, except on his specific orders, and he was the one not to ever issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any fire from that part of the town targeting the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the deployment of the BH army and its corps, or support equipment, including mortars of all calibres, were deep into the defence area of the corps. If the line was here on Colina Kapa, Rastovac and other features, then the mortars positioned not far away from Bascarsija were firing at our positions, and we were not allowed to respond because we would have destroyed this cultural and historical area and bring about condemnation by the international community and the United Nations. They used this in a very ingenious way in order to try and place blame on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask for this document to be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, reading the order from General Milosevic, it still seems to me that the order requires that a fire plan be drawn up in the region of Bascarsija and Vrbanja, and I'd like to -- to be sure that it is understood to mean that the SRK should prepare a fire plan and determine certain targets within Bascarsija. Is that correctly understood, that the idea of this order was to actually to target houses in Bascarsija? Witness, can you answer that question directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was not to identify the targets. He strictly demanded, in view of the fact that it was a cultural monument, to make it clear to subordinate units, that targets in Bascarsija can be engaged only and solely on his order. There's this Vrbanja mosque crossing the Miljacka river and Bascarsija were not under any circumstances to be targeted; and if that were to happen, that could only happen on his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And do you know then if such orders were ever given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These orders were never given. Had they been given, this kind of neighbourhood built of very weak material would have been completely destroyed, and that would have been a reason for another very strong condemnation with regard to what was happening in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell me, you, nevertheless, knew where these firing positions were on the Vrbanja bridge, and the SRK also knew where these positions were, particularly since you were there since the beginning of the war. You knew where these firing positions were, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By observing from a certain part, we acquired information about the location of enemy firing positions for support. I'm referring to 82 metre, 120-millimetre, and 60-millimetre mortars. Most of them were deployed in the inner-city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come to that later.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cengic Vila, Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. What I wanted to ask you to tell the Judges: Even if you knew where these firing positions relating to Bascarsija were, was there ever any order issued to fire upon Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never any order issued to fire any heavy weaponry on Bascarsija, Cengic Vila, or any part of the town, except on the separation line and military positions. Mortars were used to target military position, but there was a strict ban referring to all other parts, not only Bascarsija, but Bascarsija was particularly stressed because of its cultural and historical importance. It was so important that there was no target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm going to ask the witness whether this was an offensive plan or a defensive one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from 1992 the Republika Srpska army, or, to be more specific, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, carried out only one defensive operation and that was Lukovac 1993. All the other offensive actions, we actually did not carry out any other offensives. We only defended ourselves until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand that because the transcript says that, from 1992, the Republika Srpska army, or more specifically the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, carried out only one defensive operation, and that was Lukovac 1993; and then your last sentence was: "We only defends ourselves until the end of the war." So could you just clarify the answer for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness, as far as I was able to understand him, because I speak the same language, he said offensive and then he corrected himself, and then he said it was defensive; and then he corrected himself and he said offensive, so, hence, this misunderstanding. The only offensive operation was Lukavica 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lukovac, 1993. The only time when we launched an attack was in 1993 when we carried out Lukovac Operation. For the rest of the time, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps defended itself against the 1st Corps of the BH army, which launched several offensive operations: The Death and Life Operation, Koverat 1, Koverat 2, and then the last one was T-95 Operation here in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your answer covers the period 1994 and 1995, as well as 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to tell me when the 1st Romanija Brigade moved to other positions from the positions that it manned until 1993?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Romanija Brigade, following Lukovac 1993 Operation, once this position here was broken, moved from Jahorina. One of its battalions moved up to Bjelasnica and to positions above Igman; and then in the spring of 1994, it was tasked with taking up to the positions up here at Niksic plateau, from the village of Ajdanovici to the village of Kridinici. So these were just the two battalions in 1994 and in November --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to answer your question for me to continue. What happened at the Niksic plateau in 1994? Why did you have to move two battalions to that location? So now I'm talking about 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in February, a demilitarised zone was established, following the signing of an agreement, and the heavy weapons had to be moved away from the city of Sarajevo to a line 20 kilometres from the city centre, and all the artillery had to move to those positions and placed under the control, and that went both for the artillery of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS and the 1st Corps of the BH army. The corps forces -- well, in fact, it benefitted the 1st Corps most, because they knew that the agreement had been signed, that there would be no fighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, how does what happened in the Niksic plateau in 1994 impinge on the location identified in the indictment, which is Sarajevo? This raises a question of relevance, and that's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, was the Niksic plateau within this area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after the heavy weapons had been moved out or placed in storage? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, in February, agreement was signed stipulating that all heavy weapons had to be moved out of a zone, defined in the agreement to an area 20 kilometres away from the city centre. That went for both party, both warring factions, and these weapons had to be placed under the control of UNPROFOR. So the heavy weapons could not be used. There was a prohibition on the use of happy weapons, and all fighting was prohibited in a 20-kilometre zone. The forces of the 1st Corps of the BH army utilized their human resources potential, moving those forces out of the city through the airport tunnel deploying them on various areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This may be a procedural misunderstanding. I asked you, Mr. Tapuskovic, to explain the relevance of evidence relating to the Niksic plateau, the relevance to the indictment which is concerned principally with Sarajevo, but you don't answer my question by asking the witness further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, let me explain to you. You know that a witness, who was not a protected witness, came here to give evidence. It was a high-ranking officer from the BH army, the only such personage to give evidence here, and he testified that after the zone of exclusion of heavy weapons was established that the 1st Corps of the BH army employed the following tactics: They would move their fresh troops through the tunnel and attack Ilidza, Ilijas, Vogosca, the Niksic plateau in particular, the northern part; and to the south, they would attack Trnovo, and they would provoke the other side at the lines where the heavy weapons had been moved to. This was the tactics employed by the BH army throughout the fall of 1994 from the time when Dragomir Milosevic took over the command, and it actually began in the spring of 1994, as soon as the total exclusion zone was established, and this lasted until the offensive launched in May 1995. And Witness, this witness here before us, knows a lot about those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, on the question of relevance of evidence relating to the Niksic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we also don't think it is relevant, but we have a certain understanding that the Defence, with its first witness, wants to lay out the land, so that is the reason why we didn't object that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I would like to ask you to answer as briefly as possible and as slowly as possible. I will now take you through another of documents, but we have to make sure that we don't overlap and that we use the time allotted to us as efficiently as possible. Now I have to move on to the time-period in which General Milosevic was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. You said that you knew, approximately, when he was pointed the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, first of all, what happened in this period in August 1994? What characterised this period in as simple terms as possible?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the total exclusion zone was established while General Galic was the commander, prohibiting the use of happy weaponry and the fighting in the city, the Muslim forces, the 1st Corps of the BH army, was in a favourable position because they knew that there would be no fighting in the city area, and it concentrated its forces on the Trnovo axis and the Niksic plateau in order to cut shorter this front here and to re-establish the front here at Jahorina and to connect its lines here at Pale, to put us in an untenable situation, to put in those pockets of fire. That's what they wanted to do, to make our situation even more difficult than it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were the casualties, both civilian and military, in this period?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lives of soldiers and civilians in this period were lost in the Trnovo theatre of war and in the Niksic plateau and a small part of the Ilijas theatre. All the other areas, the Serbian Ilidza, Grbavica, Nedzarici, and in particular this densely populated area, they were protected. This is where the 1st Corps was positioned, and this is where most of the people were concentrated, the highest density of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's DD00-264 -- 2462.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please explain to the Judges very slowly where does this document originate from, what is the date, what are its contents? So could you please answer these questions. Three questions, but you can answer them once you've had a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces. The date is the 1st of November, 1994. It's a report on great combat achievements of the 1st Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it now. This document was signed by the commander of the Main Staff, of the General Staff; in other words, that was General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All those things that you described to us regarding the fighting, does this correspond what it is says here in the first paragraph of this document. Could you please read it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. "In the last few days, the units of the -- units and commands of the 1st Corps continued combat operations in the areas of Bjelasnica and Treskavica towards Trnovo and Roboj and made great achievements in liberating the territory and seizing war booty, which consisted of combat equipment unprecedented in quantity and usefulness."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what units they used to achieve those results?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as can you see from this text, those units were the units of the 1st Corps of the BH army in the areas that I just specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the fourth paragraph, and in fact if can you read it.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. "The 1st Corps units have been reinforced by war booty as follows: 70, 55 tanks; 122-millimetre self-propelled Howitzer; five armoured transporters; five different types of cannon; two anti-aircraft guns; five anti-aircraft machine-guns; 12 different calibres mortars; six anti-aircraft rockets."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Seven trucks, a water tank truck, a bus, a large number of luxury cars, and large amount of different calibre infantry and artillery ammunition."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this was in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now let us move on to the penultimate paragraph, if you can just read it. Can you see it, and does this correspond to the events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the one starting with "I congratulate"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I congratulate the brave fighters an officers" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Go slowly.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I congratulate the brave soldiers and officers, all units and commands of the 1st Corps for taking a direct part in the planning, preparation, and carrying out of combat operations that produced such results."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this something that, in fact, was the dominating feature of the fall of 1994?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, in light of the fact that the demilitarised zone was used to attack the flanks in order to achieve those results, because they knew that the 1st Corps of the Republika Srpska army would not be able to respond and to try and link up the front line here in the city area. And, in fact, they used their superiority in personnel to achieve those results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any combat at the other separation lines after all, the one us that referred to just now?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only from time to time, and individually. We soldiers called this sporadic gun-fire. It came from town, so that they would in this way engage part of our forces; and since we did not have a great deal of manoeuvring force, we did not manage to appose them at the flanks, in view of the high personnel levels of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when that period elapsed, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When that period elapsed - again, I'm referring to the period of 1994 that elapsed - we were in an unfavorable position on our flanks. Also, at the Niksic plateau, there was some movement and all conditions were created for fully destroying the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the population that lived in the area. In 1994, on the 23rd of December, a new agreement was signed about total cessation of hostilities; and for the duration of four months, from the 1st of January, 1995, up to the month of April, or rather, the 1st of May, 1994, this was a cease-fire on all fronts in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. Politicians signed this, and the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic, most probably with the commander of the Main Staff or his envoy, on the 31st of December, 1994, signed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't really need all those details. Tell me now, what was this four-month period like? Up to the month of May, what happened during that period?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the front of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the 1st Corps, up until the end of April, it was calm most of the time, expect for sporadic fighting, and the preparations of both armed formations to train further; whereas, in other areas, especially the Vlasic area towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We're not interested in that here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't. We don't have time for that. Now tell me briefly, when was it that you arrived at the Main Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, not the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I arrived there on the 19th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you briefly describe what the chain of command looked like in that situation when you arrived there? I mean, you were there at headquarters, right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did things look like?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters, the staff, was staffed only by one-fifth; that is to say, only 20 per cent of the necessary personnel, and that is the way things remained all the way up to the end of the war. At the head of the corps was General Milosevic. We issued orders to tour units in order to have the cease-fire observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued these orders?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff issued these orders, and the orders were carried out by the commander towards his subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In these conditions of war, what was the authority vested in individual commanders at levels below the level of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authority of the commanders of the lower ranking units, after the cease-fire agreement was signed, were non-existent in their combat zones respectively until they would receive orders from the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the role of the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the liaison officer, what I know about that is that liaison officers were in the same building where we were. And from time to time when Brigade commanders reported at the staff, they would also come from time to time to report; and most probably, they directly reported the corps commander, but I did not know about everything that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, lest I forgot. The document DD00-2462, I would like to have it admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether you remember when you attended these talks between Milosevic and the liaison officers? Can you remember any of this? What was discussed primarily?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was discussed primarily were certain meetings that were being scheduled, and then also helicopter flights by UN officers so that fire would not be open, then also to allow free passage to humanitarian convoys through our attempts, also not to have roundabout roads taken, then also have to wounded persons from the protected areas like Grdonj to be transported into Sarajevo for treatment. That's about it. I didn't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your duty? What was it that you did?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was operations officer in the corps. In the Corps Staff, I was subordinated to the Chief of Staff of the corps to the deputy commander of the commander; that is to say, General Milosevic, and that was Commander Cedomir Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you did specifically? Did you have any particular task?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations department where we conducted teaching and training for improving the units and collecting combat documentation; and then after that, according to this combat documentation, we planned our Defence, and the commander and others would make certain corrections in those plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you use this cease-fire for some kind of preparations and for training your men?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm going to show you a Prosecution Exhibit, P680, which is on the 65 ter list of the Defence, so P680 is the number. Can you take a look at this? Can you tell us whose document this is, what the date is, and what this pertains to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The 5th of January, 1995 is the date. Drafting of the order for training in 1995, order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Do you see this note up here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- well, actually don't give any answers before I finish my question. Can you see this note? What does this note state?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This note is addressed to the operations officer, to me, to Major Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to these instructions, what were you supposed to be do?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read the first paragraph, and then it is going to be a bit clearer. You moved this a bit, so it's not very good. This is what it says: "Pursuant to the instructions for training in 1995, and -- or rather, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential, number 03/4-2571/94. And in order to thoroughly and realistically plan the substance and forms of training in 1995, as well as to meet the deadlines set in the Main Staff instruction, I hereby" -- I can explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please explain what it was that you were supposed to do, but as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My operations organ was supposed to carry out the teaching, and this had to do with everything in relation to our life, work, and teaching there. And at every moment the army had to carry out training every year. The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska is the creator of this training; and on the basis of its order, on the basis of the order of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, all subordinate units --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- have to carry out training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this particularly pertain to all units in the actual sense of the word or to the weapons used by the units?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in all corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wait for my question. Wait until you see it there, and then give me your answer. Can you answer this question for me?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of all the corpses of the army of Republika Srpska, training was carried in accordance with the order issued by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For what particular weaponry, if you can tell me?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of planning, training, we would reduce some of the training into brigade level, battalion level, company level, and certain types of training are carried out by the command itself, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit as well? Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. It's already a Prosecution Exhibit. Thank you. Well, it's already a Prosecution Exhibit. Now I would like to put yet another Prosecution Exhibit to the witness, P683 -- or rather, P684.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you have a look at this document quickly, briefly, tell us what this is, whose document, what's the date, and what is its essence? I don't want to dwell on it very long.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed this and this other person typed it out, if you see this SV and the other initials. So I worked on drafting on this document. It was signed by General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, please. Since we're talking about documents anyway, a proper document, what does a proper document contain?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A proper document contains the information on who it was that dictated the document, who typed it out on a typewriter, and who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who drafted this document, and what does this pertain to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me, SV, Stevan Veljovic, and the typist, and the document was signed by Dragomir Milosevic, commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it contains?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please just be moved down a bit, so that I see the document? "The commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, strictly confidential, number 20/04-20, the 19th of January, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please. Try just to read it, and tell what you say this is.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order on assigning and dispatching sniper instructors for training at the Jahorina barracks. It's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There. Now who organised it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This corps was organised -- this course was organised by the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training snipers, sniper instructors, for carrying out their combat tasks at the separation lines, since they were highly untrained and they did not know how to use -- well, I mean, the teaching organ of the Main Staff attempted to carry out this training of sniping instructions, because it was only soon after the conflict broke out that snipers were introduced and many people did not each know what a sniper was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of tasks for what kind of tasks?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, strictly military tasks, and one knows what it is that soldiers who are snipers are supposed to, to destroy military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that was already admitted -- that has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, while you were in this position that you were in, what can you tell me about General Dragomir Milosevic? Where was he most of the time, and what was it that he did?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dragomir Milosevic was commander of the corps and he was in charge of the units of the command, and he was made in charge by the Main Staff. He was at the command post in Lukavica, and then he was at forward composts in Trnovo and at the Niksic plateau. And everywhere he was he was, as a rule, at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where he spent most of his time? Please look at the typing.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spent most of his time touring units and positions, and he would invariably return to the command post in Lukavica or the two forward command posts towards the Niksic plateau or Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any of his orders, and what did his orders pertain to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the corps was in a very difficult position, it had suffered enormous losses in the preceding period of the war, his position was that the corps should take defensive positions and that it should be properly fortified because we were expecting that the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would attack us any minute. And wherever he went, he spoke to soldiers and officers at these positions and said that fire should only be opened at enemy soldiers and no one else, and that they had to pay particular attention to fire coming from heavy weapons, and this pertained to the weapons of the other side. And the Geneva Convention had to be observed at all costs because he said that there is responsibility after every war and probably this one, too, and that is what he would say to his soldiers. And at a front line this big, perhaps there were some omissions that he could not have prevented because people in these units had different kinds of problems and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Could you now please explain to the Trial Chamber, especially this period from January up to May. Did you have information about this, what the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would do?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of information?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH army had violated the truce. In February 1995, they carried out the Vlasic Operation. It was a broad operation aimed at the 1st Corps of the VRS towards Banja Luka, and they achieved significant result by capturing Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we had information that there was a impending attack on us because the BH army was preparing such an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Describe for us this period between January and May at the command post and at these specific positions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the truce around Sarajevo is concerned, it was more or less observed by both parties until May, except for some sporadic incidents that were not of any major significant. But the units on both side, that is our corps and their side as well, were conducting training. They are training for offensive operations, and we were training for defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what started happening in early May?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early May, units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina resumed intensive fighting in the area Treskavica and Trnovo front from the town towards Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now document DD00-195 [as interpreted]. And if you please can just take a look at it and tell me briefly whether this corresponds to what you just said. Please look at it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is DD00-1925.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
